analysis.one_liner: Eases how generic drugmakers get brand-name drug samples to develop cheaper copies.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, introduced in March 2023, was referred to the Senate health committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic drugmaker wants to make a cheaper copy of a brand-name drug, it often needs actual samples of that drug. Brand-name companies can slow this by refusing to sell samples, adding restrictive contract terms, or through safety programs that limit distribution. This bill would tighten the rules: it would let generic makers prove a sample request was made through a tracked delivery service, sue over more kinds of delays, make the FDA act faster (60 days instead of 120) on requests to get restricted drugs when no human trials are involved, and require brand-name companies to publicly post their policies for handling sample requests.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who pay for prescription drugs, since faster generic and biosimilar competition generally lowers prices. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers also benefit directly, because the bill gives them clearer legal tools to obtain samples and sue when brand-name companies delay.

how_it_helps.text: Lets generic developers prove they requested samples through a tracked delivery service and adds restrictive contract terms to the conduct that can trigger a civil suit against a brand-name company [S3].
Requires the FDA to authorize generic access to drugs with strict safety-distribution programs within 60 days instead of 120 when testing does not involve human clinical trials [S2].
Requires brand-name manufacturers to publicly post policies on how they evaluate and respond to sample requests, including contact information and a named responsible officer [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would have to sell samples on demand, accept broader grounds for lawsuits over delays, and publish their handling policies. To the extent faster generic entry cuts into brand-name revenue, that cost is borne by the brand-name companies rather than passed to patients.

drawbacks.text: Brand manufacturers have long argued that forced sample sharing and faster generic entry can reduce the returns that fund development of new medicines; the bill widens the conditions that can trigger lawsuits and shortens FDA review timelines, though it keeps FDA authorization for requests involving human clinical trials [S2].

The bill targets one bottleneck in generic development; it would not cap drug prices or address other reasons generics are delayed, so its effect on out-of-pocket costs would likely be modest for any single drug [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The likely benefits to patients through more timely generic competition outweigh the costs to brand-name manufacturers, though the bill is a narrow fix rather than a broad price control, and some safety-protocol concerns around restricted-distribution drugs remain even as the bill preserves FDA review.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Maggie Hassan introduced the bill on March 30, 2023, joined by Sen. Mike Braun, making it a Democratic-Republican pairing from the start [S3].
One Senate Republican cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction; no further action appears in the record [S5].
No committee markup, floor vote, or passage ever occurred, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, since they keep the existing ability to delay sample requests without the new disclosure duties, shortened FDA timelines, and expanded lawsuit grounds the bill would have imposed. Patients waiting for cheaper generic versions gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to speed generic and biosimilar development by easing sample access.

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the bill was referred on March 30, 2023; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat introduced the bill and a Republican cosponsored it; there is no record of opposition votes because the bill never reached the floor.

industries.note: The bill would force them to sell samples to generic developers on request, accept broader grounds for delay lawsuits, and post their sample-request policies publicly. Their interest in resisting sample access runs against patients who want cheaper generic versions sooner.

The bill gives them faster FDA authorization for restricted drugs, proof-of-request tools, and expanded legal remedies, which lets them bring lower-priced copies to market sooner. Their gain comes through lower prices for patients.
